derivations.claim: First suppose every $q_j$ is Borel measurable. For each $j$, let $Q_j=q_j\,d\lambda$ on Borel sets; [F1, F3] makes $Q_j$ a probability measure. The function $g(n)=\prod_{r=1}^p q_{v_r}(n_{v_r})$ is Borel, hence product-measurable, by [F7, F8]. Repeated Tonelli gives $\int g\,d\rho=1$ and, on every Borel rectangle, $\int_{\prod B_j}g\,d\rho=\prod_j Q_j(B_j)$. Uniqueness of product measures identifies this Borel density measure with the joint law of the independent noises.

Recursion in topological order defines a Borel map $T:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^p$ from the noise vector to $X$. Its inverse has coordinates $n_j=x_j-f_j(x_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})$, so the observational law is the Borel pushforward under $T$.

Start from step 1.1 and change one coordinate at a time in topological order. With earlier endogenous coordinates fixed, $x_{v_r}=n_{v_r}+f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})$ is a fixed translation. Translation invariance changes its density factor to $q_{v_r}(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)}))$. Every intermediate integrand for a nonnegative Borel test function is product-measurable by [F7, F8], so Tonelli justifies the successive one-dimensional substitutions. The resulting identity $\mathbb E[h(X)]=\int h(x)p_X(x)\,d\rho(x)$ for every nonnegative Borel $h$ proves the density assertion on Borel sets. The product is Borel and strictly positive. No choice principle was used in this case.

Now assume Countable Choice and allow arbitrary Lebesgue-measurable $q_j$. By [F9] choose Borel representatives, replace their values outside $(0,\infty)$ by $1$, and call the resulting functions $\bar q_j$. Since each original density is positive and finite almost everywhere, this changes it only on a null set and preserves its integral and noise law. Choose a Borel null hull $Z_j$ of $\{q_j\ne\bar q_j\}$. These are only finitely many applications of [F9]. Step 2.1 applied to $\bar q_j$ gives the positive Borel density $\bar p_X$ relative to $\rho$.

For each $j$, let $E_j=\{x:x_j-f_j(x_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})\in Z_j\}$. It is Borel by [F8]. With all coordinates except $x_j$ fixed, its $x_j$-section is a translate of $Z_j$ and has measure zero by [F6]; for $p>1$, Tonelli gives $\rho(E_j)=0$, and for $p=1$ this follows directly from translation invariance. Off the finite union $E=\bigcup_jE_j$, the products $p_X$ and $\bar p_X$ agree. Completeness [F10] therefore makes $p_X$ measurable for $\bar\rho$, with the same integral on every completed measurable set as $\bar p_X$. Every original factor is positive, proving strict positivity as well.

In the Countable Choice case, the density measures in steps 2.1 and 4.1 extend the Borel observational law. To see uniqueness among absolutely continuous extensions, first note that every product-measurable set differs from a Borel set by a subset of a Borel $\rho$-null set: the sets with this property form a sigma-algebra under Countable Choice and contain every Lebesgue rectangle by [F9]; Borel null coordinate slabs have product measure zero by Tonelli. A product-null set has a Borel null hull by the same representation, so every $\bar\rho$-measurable set has such a representation too. Any absolutely continuous extension assigns zero to the exceptional set and is determined by the Borel core. Thus the stated extensions and both density conclusions hold.

topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$; every arrow points from an earlier to a
later vertex. For $j\in V$, let
$\operatorname{pa}(j)=\{i\in V:(i,j)\in E\}$ be its parent set, and let
$\operatorname{nd}(j)$ be the vertices other than $j$ that are not descendants
of $j$. A **continuous additive-noise model** on $G$ consists of real random
variables $X_j,N_j$ on a common probability space and continuous Borel
functions $f_j:\mathbb R^{\operatorname{pa}(j)}\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$$

independent, and each $N_j$ has a strictly positive Lebesgue density $q_j$.
All vertices of $G$ are observed; no latent vertices are omitted from the
model. The **observational law** is the law of the vector

The model is **causally minimal** when every parent input is essential: for
each edge $i\to j$, there are values of the other parent coordinates and two
distinct real values of the $i$-coordinate at which $f_j$ takes different
values. A root has no parent-coordinate minimality condition.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let a finite additive-noise model have topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$,
equations $X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$, and strictly positive
Lebesgue densities $q_j$ for its mutually independent noises. Write
$\rho=\lambda^{\otimes p}$ for the finite product of one-dimensional Lebesgue
measure. If all $q_j$ are Borel measurable, the observational law has the
strictly positive Borel density
$$p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
with respect to $\rho$ on Borel sets.

For arbitrary Lebesgue-measurable $q_j$, assume Countable Choice. There are
strictly positive finite Borel density versions $\bar q_j=q_j$ almost
everywhere. Their product
$$\bar p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p \bar q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
is a strictly positive Borel density with respect to $\rho$. The original
product $p_X$ is measurable for the completion $\bar\rho$ of $\rho$, agrees
with $\bar p_X$ $\bar\rho$-almost everywhere, and is a strictly positive
density with respect to $\bar\rho$. In this Countable Choice case, on non-Borel sets these density measures
refer to the unique absolutely continuous extensions of the Borel
observational law to the indicated sigma-algebras.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For disjoint $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, $C$ d-separates $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ if and
only if deleting $C$ from $\operatorname{mor}_G(X\cup Y\cup C)$ leaves no
undirected path from $X$ to $Y$.

For $S\subseteq V$, its **ancestral set** is
$$\operatorname{An}_G(S):=\{v\in V:\text{there is a directed path from }v\text{ to some }s\in S\},$$
where paths of length zero are allowed, so $S\subseteq\operatorname{An}_G(S)$.
The induced directed subgraph on this set keeps exactly the arrows of $G$
whose two endpoints lie in $\operatorname{An}_G(S)$. Its **moral graph** is
the undirected simple graph obtained by replacing every arrow by an
undirected edge and joining every distinct pair of parents of a common child
by an undirected edge; loops and duplicate edges are discarded. This
undirected graph is the **ancestral moral graph** on $S$ and is denoted
$\operatorname{mor}_G(S)$.

derivations.claim: For Borel noise densities use the displayed product. Otherwise [F1] supplies positive finite Borel versions under the assumed Countable Choice; use their Borel product throughout the integrations below. It has the same observational law, and its marginal densities agree almost everywhere with the stipulated marginal versions, so the final almost-everywhere identity transfers to those versions. Put $H=\operatorname{An}_G(A\cup B\cup C)$. No vertex outside $H$ is a parent of a vertex in $H$, since that would make it an ancestor of $A\cup B\cup C$. Integrate the product density [F1] over $V\setminus H$ in reverse topological order. At each elimination, all child factors have already been integrated and no child lies in $H$, so the only remaining factor involving the current coordinate $x_v$ is $q_v(x_v-f_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)}))$. Its section integral is one by [F2]. Tonelli [F3] justifies each section integral; consequently the marginal density on $H$ is $\prod_{v\in H}q_v(x_v-f_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)}))$.

By [F4], deleting $C$ from the moral graph on $H$ leaves no path from $A$ to $B$. Partition its connected components into $L$, the union of components meeting $A$, and $R$, the union of the remaining components. Then $A\subseteq L$, $B\subseteq R$, and there is no moral edge between $L$ and $R$. For each $v\in H$, the factor indexed by $v$ in step 1.1 depends only on $\{v\}\cup\operatorname{pa}(v)\subseteq H$; this set is a clique in that moral graph by [F5]. Hence no such factor involves both an $L$-coordinate and an $R$-coordinate. Assign factors involving an $L$-coordinate to $U$, and assign all other factors to $W$. Their finite products give a factorization of the density on $H$ as $U(x_L,x_C)W(x_R,x_C)$.

Integrate the factorization in step 2.1 over the hidden coordinates $L\setminus A$ and $R\setminus B$. Since the factors separate and are nonnegative, Tonelli [F3] yields measurable functions $u(x_A,x_C)$ and $w(x_B,x_C)$ such that $p_{A\cup B\cup C}(x_A,x_B,x_C)=u(x_A,x_C)w(x_B,x_C)$ almost everywhere. Each function is strictly positive because it integrates a strictly positive factor over its hidden coordinates; if that coordinate set is empty, it is the original strictly positive factor.

Define $\alpha(x_C)=\int u(x_A,x_C)\,dx_A$ and $\beta(x_C)=\int w(x_B,x_C)\,dx_B$. Tonelli makes these measurable and gives $p_{A\cup C}=u\beta$ and $p_{B\cup C}=w\alpha$ almost everywhere. Also $p_C(x_C)=\int u(x_A,x_C)w(x_B,x_C)\,dx_A dx_B$ for almost every $x_C$. The marginal $p_C$ is positive, since it integrates the everywhere-positive density over any unit box in the remaining coordinates, and it is finite almost everywhere since $\int p_C=1$. For almost every such $x_C$, strict positivity of $u,w$ gives $\alpha,\beta>0$. If, for example, $\alpha=\infty$, then $\beta>0$ supplies a set of $b$-values of positive measure where $w(b,x_C)>1/n$ for some $n$, so Tonelli makes $\int u(a,x_C)w(b,x_C)\,da\,db=\infty$; the same argument applies if $\beta=\infty$. Let two finite causally sufficient additive-noise models on distinct DAGs
with the same vertex set have the same observational law, a strictly positive
joint density, and causal minimality in each model. If their DAGs are $G$ and $G'$, then there
are vertices $y,l$ and a set $S$ such that $y\to l$ in $G$, $l\to y$ in $G'$, and
$$\operatorname{pa}_G(l)\setminus\{y\}\subseteq S\subseteq \operatorname{nd}_G(l)\setminus\{y\},\qquad \operatorname{pa}_{G'}(y)\setminus\{l\}\subseteq S\subseteq \operatorname{nd}_{G'}(y)\setminus\{l\}.$$

In a finite additive-noise model on a DAG $G$, for every vertex $j$ and every
set $S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)$ of nondescendants, the noise $N_j$ is
independent of the random vector $X_S=(X_k)_{k\in S}$.

For a smooth bivariate additive-noise model $Y=f(X)+N$, let $f$ be three
times continuously differentiable, and let $X$ and $N$ have strictly positive
three-times continuously differentiable densities $p_X$ and $p_N$. Put
$\xi(x)=\log p_X(x)$ and $\nu(z)=\log p_N(z)$. The triple $(f,p_X,p_N)$
satisfies **Condition 19** when there are $x,y\in\mathbb R$ with
$\nu''(y-f(x))f'(x)\ne0$ at which
$$\xi'''(x)\ne \xi''(x)\left(-\frac{\nu'''(y-f(x))f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))}+\frac{f''(x)}{f'(x)}\right) -2\nu''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x) +\nu'(y-f(x))f'''(x) +\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))\nu'''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))} -\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))(f''(x))^2}{f'(x)}.$$
Here every derivative of $\nu$ is evaluated at $y-f(x)$ and every derivative
of $f$ at $x$. The nonzero-domain condition makes both denominators in this
formula well defined.

A finite additive-noise model is a **restricted additive-noise model** when
every structural function $f_j$ is $C^3$ and every noise has a strictly
positive $C^3$ Lebesgue density, and when for every vertex $j$, every parent
$i\in\operatorname{pa}(j)$, and every set
$S$ satisfying
$$\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}\subseteq S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)\setminus\{i\},$$
there is a value $s$ with $0<p_S(s)<\infty$ such that the
conditional law of $X_i$ given $X_S=s$, together with the structural slice
$u\mapsto f_j(s_{\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}},u)$ and the noise $N_j$,
is a smooth bivariate additive-noise model satisfying Condition 19. The
conditional density is the ratio
$p_{X_i,X_S}(u,s)/p_S(s)$ for the finite positive-density version supplied
by the joint-density formula. The structural slice and conditional input
density have the smoothness and strict positivity required in the preceding
Condition 19 definition. If the model has no edges, the restricted condition
is vacuous.

Let a finite additive-noise model have topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$,
equations $X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$, and strictly positive
Lebesgue densities $q_j$ for its mutually independent noises. Write
$\rho=\lambda^{\otimes p}$ for the finite product of one-dimensional Lebesgue
measure. If all $q_j$ are Borel measurable, the observational law has the
strictly positive Borel density
$$p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
with respect to $\rho$ on Borel sets.

For arbitrary Lebesgue-measurable $q_j$, assume Countable Choice. There are
strictly positive finite Borel density versions $\bar q_j=q_j$ almost
everywhere. Their product
$$\bar p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p \bar q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
is a strictly positive Borel density with respect to $\rho$. The original
product $p_X$ is measurable for the completion $\bar\rho$ of $\rho$, agrees
with $\bar p_X$ $\bar\rho$-almost everywhere, and is a strictly positive
density with respect to $\bar\rho$. In this Countable Choice case, on non-Borel sets these density measures
refer to the unique absolutely continuous extensions of the Borel
observational law to the indicated sigma-algebras.

Assume Countable Choice, or suppose the specified noise densities are Borel measurable.
Let a finite causally sufficient additive-noise model have graph $G$, and let
$y\to z$ be an edge such that there is no directed path from $z$ to any other
child of $y$. Write $D=\operatorname{de}_G(z)$ for the strict descendants of
$z$ and $S=V\setminus(D\cup\{y,z\})$. Use the supplied Borel noise densities, or fix positive finite Borel versions under Countable Choice, and let $p$ be their shifted-noise product density. Then
there are positive measurable functions $A(y,s,z)$ and $B(d,s,z)$ such that
$p(d,y,s,z)=A(y,s,z)B(d,s,z)$, where $A$ does not depend on $d$ and $B$ does
not depend on $y$. Use marginal density versions obtained by iterated
integration. Then
$$p_{X_D,X_y,X_S,X_z}(d,y,s,z)\,p_{X_S,X_z}(s,z)=p_{X_D,X_S,X_z}(d,s,z)\,p_{X_y,X_S,X_z}(y,s,z)$$
for almost every $(d,y,s,z)$. This is the density conditional-independence
factorization of $X_D$ and $X_y$ given $(X_S,X_z)$. Moreover, for every $s$
with $0<p_{X_S}(s)<\infty$, the conditional law of $(X_D,X_y)$ given
$X_S=s$ satisfies the density conditional-independence factorization given
$X_z$.

Let $C$ be a finite-dimensional real random vector, let $(Y,C)$ have a
strictly positive $C^3$ joint density $p(y,c)$, and let
$m:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be $C^3$. If $R=Y-m(C)$ is independent of $C$, then there are
strictly positive $C^3$ Lebesgue density versions $q_R$ and $p_C$ such that
$$p(y,c)=q_R(y-m(c))p_C(c)$$
for every $(y,c)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$.

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$. If a real number
$a$ satisfies $\mu(A+a)=\mu(A)$ for every Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R$,
then $a=0$.

Let $X,N$ be independent real random variables, let $Y=f(X)+N$, and suppose
$f\in C^3(\mathbb R)$ is nonconstant while $X$ and $N$ have strictly positive
$C^3$ Lebesgue densities. If the triple of $f$ and these two densities
satisfies Condition 19, then there is no reverse additive-noise representation
$X=g(Y)+M$ with $M$ independent of $Y$ and $g\in C^3(\mathbb R)$. No density
regularity for $M$ is assumed; the proof derives a strictly positive $C^3$
density version from the forward joint density and reverse independence. Hence
the direction $X\to Y$ is identified from the observational law among these
smooth bivariate additive-noise models.

Let $X$ follow a finite additive-noise model with a strictly positive joint
density and continuous structural functions that are causally minimal in each
parent coordinate. For positive joint densities, write
$Y\perp_d A\mid Z$ when the conditional-density factorization
$$p_{Y,A,Z}(y,a,z)p_Z(z)=p_{Y,Z}(y,z)p_{A,Z}(a,z)$$
holds almost everywhere. For every edge $i\to j$ and every set $S$ such that
$$\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}\subseteq S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)\setminus\{i\},$$
the density conditional-independence factorization
$X_j\perp_d X_i\mid X_S$ fails.

Fix a finite nonempty ordered vertex set $V$ and a population law of a real
vector $X=(X_j)_{j\in V}$ generated by an additive-noise model. A **population
regression rule** $\mathcal R$ assigns to each target $j\in V$ and predictor
set $C\subseteq V\setminus\{j\}$ a Borel function
$m_{j,C}:\mathbb R^C\to\mathbb R$. A **perfect independence oracle** returns
“independent” exactly when the tested random variable and random vector are
independent under this population law. For a given ANM, $\mathcal R$ is
**population-consistent on that model** if for every $j$ and every
$C$ with $\operatorname{pa}(j)\subseteq C\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)$,
there is a constant $c_{j,C}\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$m_{j,C}(X_C)=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+c_{j,C}\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
This consistency condition concerns only the population regression target and
does not assert a finite-sample guarantee. The procedure itself is defined for
any supplied regression rule and oracle.

RESIT takes $X$, $\mathcal R$, and the perfect independence oracle and
performs the following steps, using a fixed total order on $V$ for every tie
and loop order.

1. Set the remaining set $S:=V$ and an empty sink list. While $S\ne\varnothing$,
   for each $j\in S$ form
   $$R_j:=X_j-m_{j,S\setminus\{j\}}(X_{S\setminus\{j\}}).$$
   Retain the vertices for which the oracle declares
   $R_j$ independent of $X_{S\setminus\{j\}}$. If there is no such vertex,
   return `failure`. Otherwise choose the least retained vertex $k$, record
   the provisional parent set $\widehat{\operatorname{pa}}(k):=S\setminus\{k\}$,
   append $k$ to the sink list, and remove $k$ from $S$.
2. Reverse the sink list to obtain an order $\pi$. In that order, for each
   vertex $j$ and each candidate $\ell$ in its provisional parent set, in the
   fixed order, let
   $C:=\widehat{\operatorname{pa}}(j)\setminus\{\ell\}$ and form
   $$R_{j,\ell}:=X_j-m_{j,C}(X_C).$$
   If the oracle declares $R_{j,\ell}$ independent of the vector of all
   vertices preceding $j$ in $\pi$, delete $\ell$ from
   $\widehat{\operatorname{pa}}(j)$; otherwise retain it.
3. Return the DAG with arrow $i\to j$ exactly when
   $i\in\widehat{\operatorname{pa}}(j)$ after pruning.

derivations.claim: Suppose another causally minimal restricted ANM on the same vertices gives the same observational law but has a different DAG $G'$. By [F1], there are vertices $y,l$ and a set $S$ such that $y\to l$ in $G$, $l\to y$ in $G'$, and $S$ contains the other parents of $l$ in $G$ and is contained in its nondescendants; also $S$ contains the other parents of $y$ in $G'$ and is contained in its nondescendants.

Consider Phase 1 on a current vertex set $J$ obtained by deleting true sinks. A deleted sink cannot be a parent of a remaining vertex, so $J$ is parent-closed and its marginal law is the ANM product over $J$ by [F4]; consequently every original directed path between vertices still in $J$ stays in $J$. A finite DAG on nonempty $J$ has a sink $j$. Every other current vertex is a nondescendant of $j$ in the original graph: if one were a descendant, its path from $j$ would remain in the parent-closed current graph, contradicting that $j$ is a sink there. Thus for $C=J\setminus\{j\}$, $\operatorname{pa}(j)\subseteq C\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)$.

Both models in step 1.1 are restricted ANMs. By [F3] their structural functions and noise densities are $C^3$, so the product density versions supplied by [F4] are $C^3$. Since the models have the same observational law, these continuous densities agree almost everywhere and hence everywhere; denote their common pointwise version by $p$. Define the marginal versions needed below by iterated integration of this same $p$, and define conditional-density versions at each finite positive value of $p_{X_S}$ by the corresponding ratios. Apply the restricted-model definition in $G$ to the edge $y\to l$ and this exact set $S$. It supplies $s$ with $0<p_{X_S}(s)<\infty$ such that the pair $Y^*=X_y\mid X_S=s$, $L^*=X_l\mid X_S=s$, using these common density versions, is a smooth bivariate ANM satisfying Condition 19. In particular, the definition gives the forward equation $L^*=f_l(s_{\operatorname{pa}(l)\setminus\{y\}},Y^*)+N_l$ with $N_l$ independent of $Y^*$.

Population consistency gives $m_{j,C}(X_C)=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+c_{j,C}$ almost surely, so the tested residual is $N_j-c_{j,C}$. By [F2] it is independent of $X_C$, and the perfect oracle accepts $j$. Hence every iteration has at least one accepted candidate and cannot return failure.

In $G'$, the reverse edge is $l\to y$ and $S$ contains all other parents of $y$. Since $S\cup\{l\}\subseteq\operatorname{nd}_{G'}(y)$, [F2] gives $N'_y$ independent of $(X_l,X_S)$. Let $q_{N'_y}$ be its density and choose the product density version $$p_{N'_y,X_l,X_S}(n,l,s):=q_{N'_y}(n)p_{X_l,X_S}(l,s),$$ using the common marginal version fixed in step 2.1. Because $0<p_{X_S}(s)<\infty$, dividing this version by $p_{X_S}(s)$ shows that, conditional on $X_S=s$, $N'_y$ and $X_l$ are independent. The reverse structural equation at that section is $$Y^*=g_y(s_{\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(y)\setminus\{l\}},L^*)+N'_y,$$ and its structural slice is $C^3$ by [F3]. In the $G'$ product-density formula, the factor for $X_y$ depends only on $y,l,s$, because all other parents of $y$ lie in $S$; integrating the remaining coordinates by the same iterated-integral convention in step 2.1 gives the common section density $$p_{X_y,X_l,X_S}(y,l,s)=q_{N'_y}\!\left(y-g_y(s_{\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(y)\setminus\{l\}},l)\right)p_{X_l,X_S}(l,s).$$ Thus the reverse conditional pair at this exact $s$ is formed from the same density $p_{X_y,X_l,X_S}(\cdot,\cdot,s)/p_{X_S}(s)$ as the forward pair in step 2.1. They have the same law, and this is a reverse representation forbidden by [F8], proving population graph identifiability.

Now suppose a candidate $y\in J$ is not a sink. By the current-set invariant in step 1.2, choose a child $z$ of $y$ in $G[J]$ with no directed path to any other child of $y$ in $G[J]$; finiteness and acyclicity give such a child. Let $D$ be the strict descendants of $z$ in $G[J]$ and put $T=J\setminus(D\cup\{y,z\})$. Every parent of $z$ other than $y$ lies in $T$, and $T\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(z)\setminus\{y,z\}$ in the original graph as well as in $G[J]$. The restricted condition for edge $y\to z$ and set $T$ supplies $t$ with $0<p_{X_T}(t)<\infty$ at which the conditional bivariate forward model of $Z^*=X_z\mid X_T=t$ from $Y^*=X_y\mid X_T=t$ satisfies Condition 19.

The predictor set tested for $y$ is $C=J\setminus\{y\}=T\cup\{z\}\cup D$. Suppose the oracle accepts it, and set $R_y=X_y-m_{y,C}(X_C)$. Then $R_y$ is independent of $X_C$. The current joint density is positive $C^3$ by [F3]–[F4], and $m_{y,C}$ is $C^3$ by hypothesis, so [F6] gives a pointwise density version $p_{X_y,X_C}(u,c)=q_{R_y}(u-m_{y,C}(c))p_{X_C}(c).$ By [F5], at the exact witness $t$, for almost every $(z,d)$ the conditional density of $Y^*$ given $(Z^*=z,X_D=d,X_T=t)$ does not depend on $d$. Combining this with the pointwise factorization above shows that the probability laws of $R_y+m_{y,C}(t,z,d)$ and $R_y+m_{y,C}(t,z,d')$ are equal for almost every $z,d,d'$.

If $D\ne\varnothing$, [F7] forces $m_{y,C}(t,z,d)=m_{y,C}(t,z,d')$ for almost every $(z,d,d')$. Fubini supplies a fixed $d_0$ for which $m_{y,C}(t,z,d)=m_{y,C}(t,z,d_0)$ for almost every $(z,d)$. Define $g_t(z)=m_{y,C}(t,z,d_0)$; this is $C^3$ by the Phase 1 smoothness hypothesis. If $D=\varnothing$, define $g_t(z)=m_{y,C}(t,z)$, which is also $C^3$. In either case the accepted residual equation yields $Y^*=g_t(Z^*)+R_y$ almost surely. The pointwise factorization [F6], restricted to $X_T=t$ and integrated over $X_D$, shows that $R_y$ is independent of $Z^*$ in this conditional law. This is a reverse representation of the Condition 19 pair from step 3.2, contradicting [F8]. Therefore no nonsink candidate is accepted.

Phase 1 therefore removes only true sinks. Reversing their removal order gives a topological order: for every edge $i\to j$, $j$ must be removed before $i$ while both remain, so $i$ precedes $j$ in the reversed list. The provisional parent set of each vertex is exactly the set of vertices preceding it in that order.

Fix a vertex $j$ and consider its candidate parents in the fixed loop order. We prove by induction through that list that no true parent is deleted. At a true-parent candidate $\ell$, all other true parents are still present: they were either untested or retained by the induction hypothesis. The current set $C$ contains them and is contained in the preceding vertices, hence in $\operatorname{nd}(j)\setminus\{\ell\}$. If the oracle accepted deletion, the residual $U=X_j-m_{j,C}(X_C)$ would be independent of the full preceding vector, in particular of $(X_\ell,X_C)$. Since $X_j=m_{j,C}(X_C)+U$, its conditional law given $(X_\ell,X_C)$ would not depend on $X_\ell$, yielding $X_j\perp_d X_\ell\mid X_C$. This contradicts [F9]. Thus every true parent is retained.

If the tested candidate $\ell$ is not a true parent, step 7.1 ensures that every true parent remains in the predictor set $C$ after deleting $\ell$. This set is contained in $\operatorname{nd}(j)$, so [F10] makes the residual $N_j$ minus a constant; [F2] makes it independent of all vertices preceding $j$. The oracle accepts and the algorithm deletes this superfluous edge.
Steps 7.1 and 8.1 show that pruning removes exactly the superfluous preceding vertices and retains every parent. Each returned parent set is therefore the true parent set, so RESIT returns $G$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Fix a finite DAG $G=(V,E)$ and a specified topological ordering
$v_1,\ldots,v_n$ (every arrow points from an earlier to a later vertex).
Partition $V=O\sqcup H$ into **observed** vertices $O$ and **latent** vertices
$H$. For each $v\in V$, specify a measurable state space $(S_v,\mathcal
S_v)$, a measurable exogenous space $(E_v,\mathcal E_v)$, a jointly
measurable structural function
$$f_v:\prod_{u\in\operatorname{pa}(v)}S_u\times E_v\to S_v,$$
and an exogenous random element $U_v$ with values in $E_v$. Here
$\operatorname{pa}(v)=\{u:(u,v)\in E\}$; the empty product is a singleton.
The model is **Markovian** when the finite family $(U_v)_{v\in V}$ is mutually
independent. No parametric form or distributional truth is asserted. Correlated
disturbances may be represented by adding their common causes as latent
vertices, after which the exogenous family in the expanded model is required
to be mutually independent.

Recursion in the topological order defines the endogenous random elements
uniquely by $X_v=f_v(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},U_v)$. The full-joint law is the
law of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$; the observed law is its marginal law on $O$. An
observed-only DAG factorization is asserted only when $H=\varnothing$ or when
an additional stated latent-variable condition proves it.

For $I\subseteq V$ and a value $a=(a_v)_{v\in I}\in\prod_{v\in I}S_v$,
**$do(X_I=a)$** means replace only the equations indexed by $I$ by the
constants $X_v=a_v$, leaving every other structural function and every
exogenous law unchanged. Recursion then defines counterfactual values
$X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$; the interventional law is their joint law. The
response map $(a,\omega)\mapsto X_w^a(\omega)$ is jointly measurable, by
induction through the finite topological order and joint measurability of each
$f_v$. This permits evaluation at a random treatment value, such as
$X_w^{M^a}$. When $I=\{A\}$, write $X_w^a$ for the response under
$do(A=a)$. If the factual treatment is $A$, then on $\{A=a\}$ recursion
gives $X_w=X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

For a smooth bivariate additive-noise model $Y=f(X)+N$, let $f$ be three
times continuously differentiable, and let $X$ and $N$ have strictly positive
three-times continuously differentiable densities $p_X$ and $p_N$. Put
$\xi(x)=\log p_X(x)$ and $\nu(z)=\log p_N(z)$. The triple $(f,p_X,p_N)$
satisfies **Condition 19** when there are $x,y\in\mathbb R$ with
$\nu''(y-f(x))f'(x)\ne0$ at which
$$\xi'''(x)\ne \xi''(x)\left(-\frac{\nu'''(y-f(x))f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))}+\frac{f''(x)}{f'(x)}\right) -2\nu''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x) +\nu'(y-f(x))f'''(x) +\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))\nu'''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))} -\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))(f''(x))^2}{f'(x)}.$$
Here every derivative of $\nu$ is evaluated at $y-f(x)$ and every derivative
of $f$ at $x$. The nonzero-domain condition makes both denominators in this
formula well defined.

A finite additive-noise model is a **restricted additive-noise model** when
every structural function $f_j$ is $C^3$ and every noise has a strictly
positive $C^3$ Lebesgue density, and when for every vertex $j$, every parent
$i\in\operatorname{pa}(j)$, and every set
$S$ satisfying
$$\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}\subseteq S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)\setminus\{i\},$$
there is a value $s$ with $0<p_S(s)<\infty$ such that the
conditional law of $X_i$ given $X_S=s$, together with the structural slice
$u\mapsto f_j(s_{\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}},u)$ and the noise $N_j$,
is a smooth bivariate additive-noise model satisfying Condition 19. The
conditional density is the ratio
$p_{X_i,X_S}(u,s)/p_S(s)$ for the finite positive-density version supplied
by the joint-density formula. The structural slice and conditional input
density have the smoothness and strict positivity required in the preceding
Condition 19 definition. If the model has no edges, the restricted condition
is vacuous.

Let $X,N$ be independent real random variables, let $Y=f(X)+N$, and suppose
$f\in C^3(\mathbb R)$ is nonconstant while $X$ and $N$ have strictly positive
$C^3$ Lebesgue densities. If the triple of $f$ and these two densities
satisfies Condition 19, then there is no reverse additive-noise representation
$X=g(Y)+M$ with $M$ independent of $Y$ and $g\in C^3(\mathbb R)$. No density
regularity for $M$ is assumed; the proof derives a strictly positive $C^3$
density version from the forward joint density and reverse independence. Hence
the direction $X\to Y$ is identified from the observational law among these
smooth bivariate additive-noise models.

Let a finite additive-noise model have topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$,
equations $X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$, and strictly positive
Lebesgue densities $q_j$ for its mutually independent noises. Write
$\rho=\lambda^{\otimes p}$ for the finite product of one-dimensional Lebesgue
measure. If all $q_j$ are Borel measurable, the observational law has the
strictly positive Borel density
$$p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
with respect to $\rho$ on Borel sets.

For arbitrary Lebesgue-measurable $q_j$, assume Countable Choice. There are
strictly positive finite Borel density versions $\bar q_j=q_j$ almost
everywhere. Their product
$$\bar p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p \bar q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
is a strictly positive Borel density with respect to $\rho$. The original
product $p_X$ is measurable for the completion $\bar\rho$ of $\rho$, agrees
with $\bar p_X$ $\bar\rho$-almost everywhere, and is a strictly positive
density with respect to $\bar\rho$. In this Countable Choice case, on non-Borel sets these density measures
refer to the unique absolutely continuous extensions of the Borel
observational law to the indicated sigma-algebras.
